title: Microburst cardinality econ brief
body:
Purpose:
Short working brief comparing three serving configurations along two axes: tail latency (p99) exposure during short, high-cardinality bursts and effective $/query. Intended audience: product owners, SRE on-call, and dedicated-capacity sales ops.

Context and setup (concise):
- Target workload: conversational microturns (client prompt ~45 tokens, target reply ~120 tokens).
- Burst shape: delta from 0 to 40 qps in 3s, hold 25s, decay to 0. Repeated every 4 minutes for 1 hour.
- Model variants: base (fp-like) and compact (int4-ish). Numbers reported on base unless called out.
- Configurations under test: prewarmed workers (fast-path), shared multiplex pool (mux, dynamic batching), dedicated single-slot reservations (slot). Session affinity where applicable.
- Important metric windows: ramp (0–3s), steady (6–20s), tail (last 5s of hold). We report steady and tail percentiles.

Summary of observed medians (three independent runs):
- Prewarmed fast-path (2 warm workers per replica):
  steady p50=85ms, p90=200ms, p99=480ms.
  tail p99 spike up to 620ms in one run.
  relative cost-per-1000q: baseline = $0.22.
  notes: lowest median and generally best p90; occasional p99 outliers when worker queueing occurs at burst peak.

- Shared multiplex pool (16 concurrency slots, aggressive batching):
  steady p50=160ms, p90=420ms, p99=930ms.
  tail p99 often flat near 1.0s when many short turns align; tail variance higher than other configs.
  relative cost-per-1000q: ~$0.15.
  notes: best cost efficiency; queuing/batching latency dominates tails during compressed bursts.

- Dedicated single-slot (one session-owner per GPU, conservative headroom):
  steady p50=120ms, p90=260ms, p99=700ms.
  tail p99 stable ~750ms.
  relative cost-per-1000q: ~$0.26.
  notes: predictable billing and steadier tails than mux, but more expensive per unit and worse median than prewarm.

Simple ascii visual (steady-window p99 across configs at increasing instantaneous qps):
qps     0   10    20    30    40
prewarm 120 220   360   480   520  (ms)
mux     160 300   620   870   930  (ms)
slot    130 210   430   580   700  (ms)

Estimated unit economics (ballpark USD per 1k queries, rounded):
- prewarm: $0.22 per 1k queries (amortized assuming bursts justify warm workers)
- mux:     $0.15 per 1k queries (high utilization wins)
- slot:    $0.26 per 1k queries (underutilized between bursts)

Interpretation - short takeaways:
- If product SLAs are strict on p99 (sub-600ms): prewarm dominates because it reduces scheduling and cold-queue penalties. The tradeoff is paying for idle warm capacity between bursts.
- If cost is the primary lever and p99 can be relaxed: multiplexing is attractive — it reduces $/query significantly by packing short turns into shared batches. However, tails widen and become sensitive to burst alignment.
- Dedicated slots are a middle path for customers wanting predictable invoices and simple isolation, but they do not win on either p50 or cost in the microburst pattern tested.

Micro-observations worth calling out:
- Using the compact int4 variant reduced mux p99 by ~18% on average; however, decode CPU pressure created a small number of long-tail outliers tied to host-side jitter.
- Cross-region routing (us-west -> us-east) added ~40ms median and amplified p99 by ~80–120ms; regional routing is strongly preferable for latency-sensitive flows.
- Small changes to mux batching thresholds (10ms -> 5ms) materially shifted p99: lowering batch-wait reduces tail at cost of throughput efficiency.

Recommendations (operational and product):
- Default product tier: mux with per-route burst caps and aggressive telemetry (per-batch wait histogram). Provide a documented fallback route to a compact model when queue depth triggers.
- SLO-critical customers: offer a prewarm option with adaptive cooldown (scale-to-zero after 45–90s of quiet) plus a short buffer of warm workers to absorb microbursts.
- Enterprise reserved customers: sell as slot reservations but recommend an add-on prewarm buffer for microburst exposure.

Measurement follow-ups (actionable experiments):
- Sweep longer generations (300–800 tokens) to measure whether batching amortization still favors mux or if generation length flips the ranking. Owner: Kai Park. Due: 2029-03-09.
- Add per-request batch-delay tracing in mux path to identify which requests hit the tail. Owner: Lena Thompson. Due: 2029-03-06.
- Recompute $/query with finance-validated rates and include reserved vs ondemand mismatch. Owner: Ruth Alvarez. Due: 2029-03-07.

Quick notes for slide conversion:
- Keep visuals small: one table (steady p50/p90/p99), one ascii sparkline of p99 across qps, and one $/1k bar.
- Include an appendix with raw run ids and CSVs for reproducibility.

Status: draft. Intend to refine numbers after the follow-ups and then convert to a one-pager for product and sales teams.
